title: Reframing Dark Patterns: 2025 Edition
intro: The field spent years fighting unethical design by naming it — “Roach Motel”, “Confirmshaming”, “Bait and Switch”. Naming helped at first, then became a loophole.

learn.title: Why naming stopped working
learn.text:
The idea was that catchy names would shame teams into stopping. Shared vocabulary did help.

But once a pattern has a name, teams argue about **taxonomy** instead of intent: “this isn't technically Confirmshaming.”

Meanwhile the patterns multiplied.

try.q: How does naming become a loophole?
options: Teams argue the label doesn't apply to them
Users eventually learn to recognise the names
try.explain: The debate shifts from intent to definitions.

learn.title: The principle underneath
learn.text:
**Every dark pattern removes a user's ability to act freely.**

Three questions: Can they stop? Can they undo? Can they refuse?

If any answer is “no”, it's already veering into manipulation — whatever the pattern is called.

try.q: Which three questions test a pattern?
try.explain: The principle is user control and freedom.

learn.title: Accessibility is the canary
learn.text:
Dark patterns hurt users with disabilities first and hardest: a timed offer that can't be paused, a close button too small to hit, consent flows that can't be completed by keyboard.

If a pattern fails for them, it's usually taking control away from everyone.

try.q: Why does the article call accessibility “the canary in the coal mine”?
options: Patterns that remove control break there first
Automated accessibility audits catch them reliably
try.explain: It is the earliest visible symptom of a control problem.

test.q: What is the article's proposed replacement for naming?
options: A principle grounded in user control
A public register of repeat offenders
Easy to enter, very hard to leave
An offer whose timer expires on refresh
test.explain: Subscription flows are the classic example.

options: Making the decline option insulting to choose
Emailing users who abandon a cart to shame them

test.q: What did naming achieve, according to Calabro?
options: It had no effect at all
test.explain: The problem is that it stopped there. By creating shared vocabulary.
